Lecture 12 · Hierarchical clustering · Mon 9 Nov

- Agglomerative clustering merges the two closest groups, over and over — the record is the dendrogram
- Linkage is the choice that changes everything: single chains, complete and Ward make compact groups
- Height is distance. **The tree is not the answer; the cut is**

## The table

::: {.subtitle-frame}
`customers.csv` — on Blackboard, folder *Prof. Salvini*, and linked from the schedule
:::

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | customer |
| `recency` | days since last purchase |
| `frequency` | purchases in the last 12 months |
| `monetary` | total spend, last 12 months (€) |
| `tenure` | months since first purchase |
| `returns` | items returned, last 12 months |
| `channel_online` | share of purchases made online |

6 000 rows. Save it in your project's `data/` folder, then open the project.

## [Section 1]{.section-kicker} Load and look {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Step 1 — read it, then read it

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-3|5|7|9"}
library(tidyverse); library(cluster); library(factoextra); library(here)

cust <- read_csv(here("data", "customers.csv"))

glimpse(cust)               # types right? id is not a feature

summary(cust)               # ranges, NAs, and the first surprise

cust |> select(-id) |> pivot_longer(everything()) |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40) + facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free")
```

Before any model: what does `monetary` look like? Spending is almost always skewed — a few customers spend many times the median, and k-means will build a cluster around them alone.

## [Drill 1]{.drill-kicker} What `summary()` is telling you

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · `summary(cust)` and `sapply(cust[-1], sd)`, five of the six columns
:::

| Column | Min | Median | Mean | Max | SD |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `recency` | 0 | 35 | 67.2 | 391 | 80.5 |
| `frequency` | 1 | 9 | 8.68 | 27 | 5.28 |
| `monetary` | 41 | 568 | 797 | 9 214 | 812 |
| `tenure` | 1 | 42 | 40.8 | 125 | 25.4 |
| `channel_online` | 0 | 0.35 | 0.41 | 1 | 0.32 |

1. Which column would own an unscaled distance? Which number in the table says so?
2. Is `monetary` skewed? Name the two numbers that say it.
3. Any rows that are not customers — test accounts, `monetary = 0` with `frequency = 12`? Then decide what `monetary` needs before k-means, in one sentence.

## [Drill 1 · answer]{.drill-kicker} Log it, then scale everything

- **`monetary` owns the distance**: SD 812, against 80.5 for `recency` and 0.32 for `channel_online` — 99% of the total variance. Unscaled, k-means cuts spending bands and ignores the rest
- **Skewed**: mean 797 against a median of 568; the top customer spends 9 214, 16 times the median. The top 10% of customers hold 34% of all spending
- **Not customers**: none here — no `NA`, nobody under €41 or one purchase. Checked, not assumed

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"`monetary` goes in logged, and every column goes in scaled: raw, it is 99% of the distance, and its tail would get a cluster of its own — the three people who bought a car."
:::

## [Section 2]{.section-kicker} Prepare {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Step 2 — transform, then scale

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-4|6-7|9"}
feat <- cust |>
  select(-id) |>
  mutate(monetary  = log1p(monetary),        # tame the tail
         frequency = log1p(frequency))

X <- scale(feat)                              # mean 0, sd 1, every column
attr(X, "scaled:center")                      # keep these: you need them to profile

colMeans(X) |> round(3)                       # all zero. Good.
```

- `log1p`, not `log`: these two columns have no zeros, but most real tables do, and `log(0)` is `-Inf`
- `scale()` because distance in euros² + distance in days² is not a distance

## [Drill 2]{.drill-kicker} Step 2 on a patient table

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · an invented registry extract: 5 000 adult patients, one year
:::

| Column | Min | Median | Mean | Max | SD |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `gp_code` | 1001 | 1022 | 1021.6 | 1042 | 12.1 |
| `age` | 19 | 53 | 54.1 | 96 | 17.2 |
| `gp_visits` | 0 | 2 | 2.73 | 19 | 2.82 |
| `ed_visits` | 0 | 0 | 0.48 | 17 | 1.12 |
| `cost` (€) | 0 | 430 | 1 100 | 27 150 | 2 352 |

1. One column must leave before any distance, and R will not warn you. Which, and why?
2. Which columns get `log1p`, and why not `log` on this table?
3. Age: in the distance, or only in the profile afterwards? Defend it in one sentence.

## [Drill 2 · answer]{.drill-kicker} Prepare for the question you will ask

- **`gp_code` leaves**: a label stored as a number. Scaled, it would weigh as much as `age`, and GP 1001's patients would be "far" from GP 1042's. It is `id` again, in disguise
- **`log1p` on `cost` and `ed_visits`**: the top cost is 63 times the median, 17 ED visits against a median of 0. And zeros: 74% never went to the emergency department, 17% cost nothing, so `log` would return `-Inf`. `gp_visits` is borderline, either way defensible
- **Unscaled**, `cost` is 99.99% of the variance: the "segments" would be cost bands

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"Age goes in the profile, not the distance: we want groups that use care differently, and age then says who they are — so a group of young, frequent ED users can show up at all."
:::

## [Section 3]{.section-kicker} Explore {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Step 3 — a tree on a sample

Six thousand rows is $18$ million pairwise distances — fine. Sixty thousand would not be. The habit: **explore the structure on a sample, deploy on everything**.

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-2|4-5|7"}
set.seed(26)
idx <- sample(nrow(X), 1500)

hc <- hclust(dist(X[idx, ]), method = "ward.D2")
fviz_dend(hc, k = 5, rect = TRUE, show_labels = FALSE)

fviz_nbclust(X[idx, ], hcut, method = "silhouette", k.max = 8)
```

Look at the tree. Where is the big vertical gap? Two groups? Four? Six? Write down your $k$ *before* you run the silhouette, then compare.

## [Section 4]{.section-kicker} Decide and deploy {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Step 4 — k-means on everything

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-2|4|6-7"}
fviz_nbclust(X, kmeans, method = "wss", k.max = 8)        # elbow, full data
fviz_nbclust(X, kmeans, method = "silhouette", k.max = 8)

k <- 4                                        # your decision, with a reason

set.seed(26)
km <- kmeans(X, centers = k, nstart = 50)
```

Then, the test that matters more than any index:

```{.r}
set.seed(27); km2 <- kmeans(X, centers = k, nstart = 50)
table(km$cluster, km2$cluster)               # same groups, different seed?
```

If the table is not close to a permutation matrix, the structure is not stable at this $k$. Try $k - 1$.

## [Drill 3]{.drill-kicker} Four or five?

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · `kmeans(X, k, nstart = 50)` on all 6 000 rows, seed 26, and again with seed 27
:::

| $k$ | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $W$ | 23 697 | 15 822 | 10 729 | 9 270 | 8 257 | 7 751 |
| Silhouette | 0.36 | 0.42 | 0.48 | 0.47 | 0.37 | 0.34 |
| Smallest segment | 40% | 19% | 18% | 6% | 6% | 6% |
| Rows moved, seed 26 vs 27 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 712 |

1. What do the elbow and the silhouette say?
2. $k = 5$ is almost as good and just as stable. What does the *smallest segment* row add?
3. Which $k$ do you deploy? Write the sentence for the marketing director.

## [Drill 3 · answer]{.drill-kicker} Four, and why not five

- **Elbow**: $W$ falls by 12 297, 7 875, 5 093, then only 1 458 — it stops bending after $k = 4$
- **Silhouette**: best at 4 (0.48), with 5 close behind (0.47). Stability does not decide here: nothing moves between seeds up to $k = 6$; at 7, 712 rows do
- **The fifth group** is 350 customers split off segment 1 on returns alone — 3 items a year against 1. A returns policy, not a segment

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"Four: the gain in $W$ collapses after four, the silhouette peaks there, and a fifth group would be a 6% sliver of one segment, split on returns alone."
:::

## [Section 5]{.section-kicker} Profile and hand over {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Step 5 — back to the units people understand

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-2|4-8|10"}
cust$segment <- factor(km$cluster)

profile <- cust |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), share = n() / nrow(cust),
            across(c(recency, frequency, monetary, tenure, returns, channel_online),
                   ~ round(median(.x), 1)))
profile

fviz_cluster(km, data = X, geom = "point", ellipse.type = "norm")
```

Medians, not means — you logged `monetary` for a reason, and the mean is back under the tail's control.

## [Drill 4]{.drill-kicker} Name them, then spend the budget

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · your `profile` at seed 26: five of the six medians, and each segment's share of all spending
:::

| Segment | Recency (days) | Purchases | Spend (€) | Tenure (months) | Online | Customers | Of all spend |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 25 | 14 | 269 | 30 | 0.92 | 22% | 8% |
| 2 | 30 | 11 | 736 | 60 | 0.10 | 41% | 41% |
| 3 | 222.5 | 3 | 1 648 | 48 | 0.36 | 19% | 46% |
| 4 | 39 | 3 | 187 | 4 | 0.54 | 18% | 5% |

1. A **name** for each segment, from the numbers: every adjective must point at a column
2. The win-back budget goes to one segment. Which, and which number makes the case?
3. Segment 4 spends least. Do you drop it from the plan? One sentence.

## [Drill 4 · answer]{.drill-kicker} The deliverable

| Segment | Name | Who they are | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | *Online regulars* | 14 buys a year, 92% online, €269 | app push, bundles |
| 2 | *Store loyalists* | 11 buys, 10% online, 5 years | protect, no discounts |
| 3 | *Lapsed high-value* | €1 648, silent for 222 days | win-back, personal, now |
| 4 | *New and undecided* | 4 months in, 3 buys, €187 | onboarding; watch churn |

: {tbl-colwidths="[12,26,36,26]"}

- **Win-back goes to 3**: 19% of the customers, **46% of last year's spending**
- **4 stays in the plan**: it spends least because it is four months old; lecture 17's churn model says who stays
